text: Socrates was sentenced to death in Athens after a jury found him guilty of impiety and corrupting the city's youth.
context: Socrates turns questioning into a real risk: asking uncomfortable questions can threaten people who depend on obedience.
sourceNote: Britannica describes Socrates' trial, charges, conviction, and death sentence in Athens.

text: Buddha taught that suffering is tied to craving, and that changing the mind's habits can change a person's life.
context: Buddha makes inner life practical: the struggle is not only outside you, but also in what you cling to.
sourceNote: Britannica summarizes the Buddha's teaching on suffering, craving, and the path to liberation.

text: B. R. Ambedkar chaired the committee that drafted India's Constitution after spending his life challenging caste discrimination.
context: Ambedkar shows that changing a society means changing the rules that decide whose dignity counts.
sourceNote: Britannica identifies Ambedkar as a leader against caste discrimination and chairman of the drafting committee for India's Constitution.

text: Albert Einstein won the Nobel Prize for explaining the photoelectric effect, not for the theory of relativity.
context: Einstein is a reminder that public fame and the work officially recognized by history are not always the same thing.
sourceTitle: The Nobel Prize: Albert Einstein Facts
sourceNote: The Nobel Prize biography lists Einstein's 1921 prize motivation as his services to theoretical physics and discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect.

text: Rabindranath Tagore became the first non-European Nobel laureate in literature in 1913 for Gitanjali.
context: Tagore's work carried Bengali poetry into a global conversation without giving up its spiritual voice.
sourceTitle: The Nobel Prize: Rabindranath Tagore Facts
sourceNote: The Nobel Prize page records Tagore's 1913 Literature Prize and the prize motivation for Gitanjali.

text: Mahatma Gandhi turned salt into a protest symbol by walking to the sea in 1930 to challenge British colonial law.
context: Gandhi shows how a simple everyday object can become powerful when it exposes an unfair system.
sourceNote: Britannica describes Gandhi's 1930 Salt March as a nonviolent protest against the British salt monopoly.

text: Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences: Physics in 1903 and Chemistry in 1911.
context: Curie shows what disciplined curiosity can do when a person keeps asking questions after the first breakthrough.
sourceTitle: The Nobel Prize: Marie Curie Facts
sourceNote: The Nobel Prize lists Curie's Physics Prize in 1903 and Chemistry Prize in 1911.

text: Nelson Mandela spent 27 years in prison before helping lead South Africa out of apartheid.
context: Mandela's story asks whether justice can survive bitterness, waiting, and the chance for revenge.
sourceTitle: The Nobel Prize: Nelson Mandela Facts
sourceNote: The Nobel Prize biography summarizes Mandela's imprisonment and leadership against apartheid.

text: Martin Luther King Jr. was 35 when he received the Nobel Peace Prize for nonviolent civil rights leadership.
context: King shows that moral courage can become public leadership before a person feels old enough to be ready.
sourceTitle: The Nobel Prize: Martin Luther King Jr. Facts
sourceNote: The Nobel Prize page records King's 1964 Peace Prize and his age at the time.

text: Ada Lovelace wrote notes on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine that included what is often described as the first computer program.
context: Lovelace saw that a machine built for numbers could one day manipulate symbols, music, and ideas.
sourceNote: Britannica describes Lovelace's notes on the Analytical Engine and their place in computing history.

text: Alan Turing helped break German Enigma-coded messages during World War II at Bletchley Park.
context: Turing's wartime work shows how abstract logic can become a tool with real consequences for millions of lives.
sourceNote: Britannica describes Turing's work at Bletchley Park and his role in codebreaking.

text: Saint Stephen was chosen when Greek-speaking widows were being neglected in the early Jerusalem community's daily food distribution.
context: Stephen's story begins with an unfair system, not with a title or ranking.
sourceNote: Britannica describes Stephen as a deacon in Jerusalem and connects his story to Acts.

text: Aristotle taught Alexander the Great before building his own school, the Lyceum, in Athens.
context: Aristotle links two kinds of influence: shaping a ruler and building a place where ideas could keep moving.
sourceNote: Britannica summarizes Aristotle's connection to Alexander and his founding of the Lyceum.

text: Confucius taught that good government begins with moral example, not only punishment and rules.
context: Confucius makes leadership personal: people notice what leaders practice before they trust what leaders command.
sourceNote: Britannica summarizes Confucius's ethical and political teachings.

text: Swami Vivekananda introduced many Americans to Vedanta at the 1893 World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago.
context: Vivekananda shows how one speech can carry a spiritual tradition into a new public conversation.
sourceNote: Britannica describes Vivekananda's appearance at the 1893 World's Parliament of Religions.

text: Rumi's Masnavi became one of the most influential works of Persian mystical poetry.
context: Rumi shows how poetry can become a way of thinking about love, loss, discipline, and the divine.
sourceNote: Britannica identifies the Masnavi as Rumi's major work and discusses his influence.

text: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine shaped medical study in parts of Europe and the Islamic world for centuries.
context: Ibn Sina shows how organizing knowledge can change how future generations learn, diagnose, and teach.
sourceNote: Britannica describes Avicenna's Canon of Medicine and its long influence.

text: Galileo Galilei's telescope observations showed four moons orbiting Jupiter, challenging the idea that everything circled Earth.
context: Galileo Galilei shows how looking carefully can disrupt an entire worldview.
sourceNote: Britannica describes Galileo's telescopic discoveries, including Jupiter's moons.

text: Leonardo da Vinci filled notebooks with studies of anatomy, machines, water, flight, and painting.
context: Leonardo shows curiosity refusing to stay inside one subject.
sourceNote: Britannica describes Leonardo's notebooks and wide-ranging studies across art and science.

text: Marcus Aurelius wrote the reflections now called Meditations while carrying the responsibilities of a Roman emperor.
context: Marcus Aurelius shows philosophy being tested under pressure, not kept as decoration.
sourceNote: Britannica discusses Marcus Aurelius as emperor and author of the Meditations.
